answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This line comes from a private letter Lawrence wrote to his friend and literary mentor Edward Garnett in late January 1912, while convalescing from illness in Bournemouth, describing his own uneasy relationship with sleep and dreams. The exact wording is confirmed in that letter as first published in The Letters of D. H. Lawrence ↗ (1932).

source.excerpt: But at the bottom I am rather miserable. I can never decide whether my dreams are the result of my thoughts, or my thoughts the result of my dreams. It is very queer. But my dreams make conclusions for me. They decide things finally. I dream a decision. Sleep seems to hammer out for me the logical conclusions of my vague days, and offer me them as dreams. It is a horrid feeling, not to be able to escape from one’s own — what? — self-daemon — fate, or something.
trail: Written in a private letter to his friend and literary mentor Edward Garnett ↗, who at the time was Lawrence’s editor and champion at the publisher Duckworth.
Lawrence wrote the letter from Compton House in Bournemouth, where he was convalescing after a serious illness in January 1912.
First appeared in print two years after Lawrence’s death, in The Letters of D. H. Lawrence, edited by Aldous Huxley ↗ (William Heinemann, 1932).
Later re-edited from the manuscripts in the scholarly Cambridge Edition of the Letters, Volume I ↗ (1979), edited by James T. Boulton.

author.bio: David Herbert Lawrence was an English writer whose novels explored industrialization, class, and sexuality with unusual candor for his era. He is best known for Sons and Lovers, The Rainbow, Women in Love, and Lady Chatterley's Lover, and he was also a prolific letter-writer whose private correspondence is now studied as closely as his fiction.
